title: Groundwater levels in 1,576 long-record US wells did not stay low after multi-year droughts in 1951-2025: a small deficit in post-drought years 3-4 was gone by year 6
abstract: Question: do groundwater levels in long-record US wells stay lower than precipitation predicts after multi-year droughts (non-recovery or a pumping ratchet)? Approach: we used USGS field measurements of depth to water (parameter 72019) for 5,993 wells with records from before 1976 to after 2022, water-year median levels, NOAA climate-division precipitation and GHCN_CAMS temperature. Droughts are 3 or more consecutive water years below the 1951-2025 division mean with a mean deficit of 10 % or more. A reference model (precipitation lags 0-3, temperature, linear or spline trend) was fitted on normal years only. The metric is the mean standardised residual R in the 5 post-drought years. A time-shift placebo (58 common shifts) gave the null distribution. Results: for 2,579 droughts bracketed by fitted years in 1,576 wells, the mean R was -0.08 SD (linear trend, placebo 95 % range -0.21 to +0.36, p = 0.12) and -0.17 SD (spline trend, -0.30 to +0.41, p = 0.12). Across 13 variants the mean R was -0.28 to +0.19 SD. The residual was positive during droughts, lowest in post-drought years 3-4 (-0.26 to -0.38 SD, at or below the placebo 2.5th percentile) and near 0 by year 6. Thus the response was delayed, not persistent. With equal weight per division the mean R was -0.18 SD (p = 0.034, linear) and -0.12 SD (p = 0.085, spline), approximately 0.3 ft. Injected deficits of 0.25 SD in all droughts were detected in 20 of 20 draws. Wells with long-term declines and High Plains wells did not have a larger deficit; no group passed a Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Limitations: division-scale precipitation, no pumping data, model-dependent sign, an uneven well network, and some design choices made after a preliminary run on two thirds of the wells.
